title: The Executive Team's Orientation Toward Risk Can Make a World of Difference
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Drawing on Heidi Grant Halvorson and Tory Higgins' landmark book 'Focus,' this piece distinguishes two fundamental leadership orientations: promotion/opportunity focus (pursuit of advancement, growth, and gain) and preservation/stability focus (anchored in security, responsibility, and avoidance of loss). While leaders often shift orientations based on context, research consistently links opportunity-focused leadership to transformational behaviors and preservation-focused leadership to transactional behaviors. Organizations whose senior leaders maintain an opportunity focus tend to outperform peers, generating greater creativity, adaptability, and original thinking. The greatest strategic risk for senior leaders may be allowing a default orientation toward caution to dictate their most consequential decisions. High-performing organizations cultivate both orientations deliberately: preservation-focused leaders protect critical gains in appropriate functions, while senior leaders apply opportunity focus to what's possible.
points: * Promotion/opportunity-focused leadership is linked to transformational behaviors; prevention/stability-focused leadership to transactional behaviors--the distinction operates at an organizational level, shaping culture and strategic momentum. * Organizations whose senior leaders operate with an opportunity focus consistently outperform peers through greater creativity, adaptability, and willingness to challenge the industry status quo. * High-performing organizations cultivate both orientations deliberately: preservation-focused leaders protect existing gains in critical functions; senior leaders apply opportunity focus to what's possible. * In a world that rewards moving toward opportunity, the greatest organizational risk may be insufficient risk-taking caused by senior leaders defaulting to a preservation orientation. * Leaders typically have a strong preference for one orientation but often adapt to fit organizational circumstances--neither is inherently superior; context determines the right one.
quotes: Of the many differences in approach, mindset, and strategic focus that separate leaders, perhaps none is more impactful than how they view risk and opportunity.
Leaders who operate this way are energized by what could be achieved. They move eagerly toward ideals, think creatively, act quickly, and are most alive when chasing what is possible.
When a promotion or opportunity focus becomes part of the organization's culture and strategic lens, it is linked to greater creativity, adaptability, and original thinking.
What leaders cannot do, according to the research on high-performing organizations, is to allow a default orientation toward caution and loss avoidance to dictate their most consequential decisions.
In a world that now clearly rewards those who move toward opportunity, the greatest risk of all may be not taking enough of it.
